```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# Print results at most 60 characters wide, "#> " included, to fit a printed page.
options(width = 57)
# Keep the build machine out of printed query headers (load duckdb first, as it
# registers its own description when it loads).
loadNamespace("duckdb")
registerS3method("db_connection_describe", "duckdb_connection",
                 function(con, ...) "example database", envir = asNamespace("dbplyr"))
```

In the first guide you saw that `tbl()` gives a query, not a copy of the
table. This guide fills in the picture behind that: where your
code runs, which dplyr verbs and R functions work on the database, when to bring
a result into R, and how to count people when your question spans several
yearly tables.

As in [Meet the THIP data](meet-the-data.html), every example runs on the
example database of invented records. On THIP, connect with `thip_connect()`
instead and the same code runs there, apart from the differences in
[The example is DuckDB, THIP is ClickHouse](#the-example-is-duckdb-thip-is-clickhouse).
Load the packages, connect and point `stays` at the fiscal year 2567 table, as
before:

```{r connect}
library(thipR)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

con <- thip_connect_example()
stays <- tbl(con, "nhso2567")
```

## Two places

When you work with THIP there are two places. The THIP database server holds the
tables and does the heavy work. Your R session is where you write code and where
results arrive. The connection, `con`, links the two.

```{r two-places, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
# Inline, so the diagram travels with the page and keeps its title and description.
cat("```{=html}", "<div style=\"margin: 0.5rem 0 1.5rem;\">",
    readLines("figures/two-places.svg"), "</div>", "```", sep = "\n")
```

Your dplyr code is a query that waits in R. When it runs, dbplyr (the package
behind dplyr's database support) writes it as SQL, the language databases
understand, the database runs it on its
tables, and only the result travels back to R.

Build a query that counts the records of people aged 65 or over, by sex:

```{r older}
older <- stays |>
  filter(as.integer(age_y) >= 65) |>
  count(sex)
```

Nothing has run yet: `older` only describes what you want. Print it, and the
database runs it:

```{r older-print}
older
```

The database looked through the whole table, but only two rows came back to R.

The database does work at three moments:

- When you point at a table with `tbl()` or `thip_table()`, R may ask the
  database for the table's column names.
- When you print a query, the database runs it and sends back the first 10
  rows.
- When you `collect()` a query, the database runs it and sends back every row
  of the result.

Adding verbs to a query, as above, builds it in R and sends nothing.

## Verbs that run on the database

These dplyr verbs all become SQL and run on the database: `filter()`,
`select()`, `mutate()`, `summarise()` with `group_by()`, `count()`,
`arrange()`, `distinct()`, and joins between tables on the same connection.
Chain as many as you need; dbplyr writes the whole pipeline as one query.

This pipeline uses most of them. It converts age to a number, keeps people aged
65 or over and summarises their records by sex:

```{r by-sex}
by_sex <- stays |>
  select(sex, age_y) |>
  mutate(age = as.integer(age_y)) |>
  filter(age >= 65) |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarise(records = n(),
            mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(sex)

by_sex
```

The record counts match `older`:
`r format(pull(by_sex, records)[1], big.mark = ",")` men (sex 1) and
`r format(pull(by_sex, records)[2], big.mark = ",")` women (sex 2), now with
their mean age. The `# Ordered by:` line shows the `arrange()`.

`show_query()` shows the one query dbplyr wrote for it:

```{r by-sex-sql}
show_query(by_sex)
```

Read it from the inside out. The inner `SELECT`, in brackets after `FROM`,
keeps `sex` and `age_y` (`select()`) and computes `age` (`mutate()`). `WHERE`
keeps people aged 65 or over (`filter()`), `GROUP BY` with `COUNT(*)` and
`AVG()` comes from `group_by()` and `summarise()`, and `ORDER BY` from
`arrange()`. `q01` is only a name dbplyr gives the inner query, and `65.0` is
how it writes R's number 65. SQL's `AVG()` always skips missing values, so
`na.rm = TRUE` needs no SQL.

## Join tables on the same connection

Joins run on the database too, as long as both tables come from the same
connection. This one finds the people with records in both fiscal years 2566
and 2567: `distinct()` gives one row per person in each table, and
`inner_join()` keeps the people found in both.

```{r join}
people_2566 <- tbl(con, "nhso2566") |> distinct(pid)
people_2567 <- tbl(con, "nhso2567") |> distinct(pid)

in_both <- people_2566 |>
  inner_join(people_2567, by = "pid")

count(in_both)
```

The two tables never left the database; one number came back. The SQL has a
`SELECT DISTINCT` for each table and an `INNER JOIN` between them:

```{r join-sql}
show_query(in_both)
```

`LHS` and `RHS` are dbplyr's names for the left and right tables.

You cannot join a database table to a data frame in R. dplyr stops with an
error and suggests its `copy` argument, which would write your data frame to the
database or paste it into the SQL. To fetch the records of people you hold in R,
use [`thip_window()`](../reference/thip_window.html) instead
([Look back and follow up](look-back-follow-up.html)).

## R functions inside verbs

Inside `filter()`, `mutate()` and `summarise()`, dbplyr also translates R
functions into SQL. It knows the common ones: comparisons and arithmetic,
`as.integer()`, `substr()`, `toupper()`, `is.na()`, `n()`, `n_distinct()`,
`mean()` and many more. Here `as.integer()`, `substr()` and `toupper()` all
translate:

```{r translate}
stays |>
  mutate(age = as.integer(age_y),
         category = toupper(substr(pdx, 1, 3))) |>
  select(pdx, age, category) |>
  show_query()
```

`as.integer()` became `TRY_CAST(... AS INTEGER)`, `substr()` became `SUBSTR()`
and `toupper()` became `UPPER()`.

A function dbplyr does not know is copied into the SQL unchanged, and the
database looks for a function of that name. Your own R functions are the usual
case, because dbplyr cannot see inside them:

```{r own-function}
first_letter <- function(code) substr(code, 1, 1)

stays |>
  mutate(letter = first_letter(pdx)) |>
  select(pdx, letter) |>
  show_query()
```

`first_letter(pdx)` went into the SQL as written. The database has no function
called `first_letter`, so running this query stops with an error saying no
function of that name exists. Write the expression out instead:
`mutate(letter = substr(pdx, 1, 1))`.

So there are two ways to tell whether a function works on the database: read
`show_query()`, where a translated function appears under its SQL name and an
unknown one as you typed it, or run the query on a small result. Dates need
care: lubridate's `ymd()`, for one, has no translation, so convert THIP's date
text with `thip_table()`, as the next guide shows.

## The example is DuckDB, THIP is ClickHouse

The SQL in this guide is DuckDB's, the database engine behind the example. THIP
runs ClickHouse, so `show_query()` prints different SQL there, and a few
functions behave differently. `as.integer()` is one: here it becomes `TRY_CAST`,
which gives `NA` for text that is not a number; on THIP it becomes ClickHouse's
`toInt64()`, which stops with an error instead.

So on THIP, a query that converts a column stops when it meets text that is not
a number, an empty value included. If that happens, look at the values first,
for example with `stays |> count(age_y, sort = TRUE)`, and decide how to handle
them. To turn them into `NA`, write ClickHouse's own `toInt64OrNull()` in place
of `as.integer()`. dbplyr does not know this function, so it passes it to
ClickHouse unchanged, as it did with `first_letter()`. It runs only on THIP, not
on the example:

```{r to-int-or-null, eval = FALSE}
stays |>
  filter(toInt64OrNull(age_y) >= 65) |>
  count(sex)
```

Stick to ordinary dplyr verbs and the functions in dbplyr's
[translation list](https://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/translation-function.html).
When you first run a query on THIP, run it on a small result before you build
on it: running it, not reading `show_query()`, is what catches a difference
like this one.

## Bring results into R with collect()

Printing shows at most the first 10 rows; `collect()` brings the whole result
into R as an ordinary data frame (a tibble). From then on it is local data:
every R function works on it, including your own, and plots and models take it
like any other data frame. Collect the summary of older people from above:

```{r collect}
older_by_sex <- collect(by_sex)
older_by_sex
```

The header now says `A tibble: 2 × 3` rather than `A query`: the rows are in R,
and R knows how many there are.

**Collect only small results.** `collect(tbl(con, "nhso2567"))` would bring
every row and column of the table into R's memory. Filter, select and summarise
on the database first. When you are not sure how big a result is, count its rows
there before you collect it:

```{r count-first}
stays |>
  filter(as.integer(age_y) >= 65) |>
  count()
```

That is how many rows `collect()` would bring; only one number came back. On
THIP, a result larger than the connection's row or time limit stops with an
error rather than arriving cut short (see
[`thip_connect()`](../reference/thip_connect.html)); filter or summarise further
and run it again.

`DBI::dbGetQuery()`, used in the SQL tabs, works like `collect()`: it runs the
SQL at once and brings back every row. Add `LIMIT` when you only want to look.

## Count people across yearly tables {.tabset}

A question that spans several fiscal years needs several tables.
[`thip_table()`](../reference/thip_table.html) stacks them into one query, one
table under the next, and `.id` adds a column naming the table each record came
from. The next guide uses it fully; here it only stacks three years. Count
records and people in each year, then in all three together, and collect the
two small results; the SQL tab writes the yearly counts by hand, stacking with
`UNION ALL`.

### dplyr

```{r stack}
admissions <- thip_table(
  con,
  tables = c("nhso2565", "nhso2566", "nhso2567"),
  .id = "source_table"
)

per_year <- admissions |>
  group_by(source_table) |>
  summarise(records = n(), people = n_distinct(pid)) |>
  arrange(source_table) |>
  collect()
per_year

total <- admissions |>
  summarise(records = n(), people = n_distinct(pid)) |>
  collect()
total
```

### SQL

```{r stack-sql}
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT source_table, count(*) AS records,
         count(DISTINCT pid) AS people
  FROM (
    SELECT pid, 'nhso2565' AS source_table FROM nhso2565
    UNION ALL
    SELECT pid, 'nhso2566' AS source_table FROM nhso2566
    UNION ALL
    SELECT pid, 'nhso2567' AS source_table FROM nhso2567
  )
  GROUP BY source_table
  ORDER BY source_table")
```

## Records add up, people do not

The yearly records add up to the total:
`r format(sum(per_year$records), big.mark = ",")`. The yearly people do not:
they add up to `r format(sum(per_year$people), big.mark = ",")`, but there are
only `r format(total$people, big.mark = ",")` people, because many people have
records in more than one year. Count how many years each person appears in.
`distinct()` keeps one row per person per year, so `count(pid)` then counts
years, not records:

```{r years}
years_seen <- admissions |>
  distinct(pid, source_table) |>
  count(pid, name = "years") |>
  count(years, name = "people") |>
  arrange(years) |>
  collect()
years_seen
```

The `r format(years_seen$people[3], big.mark = ",")` people seen in all three
years are counted three times in the yearly sums, and the
`r format(years_seen$people[2], big.mark = ",")` seen in two years twice:
`r format(years_seen$people[1], big.mark = ",")` + 2 ×
`r format(years_seen$people[2], big.mark = ",")` + 3 ×
`r format(years_seen$people[3], big.mark = ",")` =
`r format(sum(years_seen$years * years_seen$people), big.mark = ",")`. Count
people once, with `n_distinct(pid)` on the stacked table, and never by adding
up yearly counts.

## Stacking keeps every row

`thip_table()` stacks with SQL's `UNION ALL`, which keeps every row: it does not
remove repeated records. It checks only that the tables have the same column
names and types, and stops with an error if they do not. Matching names and
types cannot tell you whether a column is coded the same way in every table, so
before you rely on a column, compare its values across `source_table`.

Stack only tables of the same kind: the yearly inpatient tables together, and
other records, such as COVID-19 vaccinations, in a query of their own. To check
that no record appears twice in the stack, see
[Check before you trust](data-checks.html#each-record-once).

## dplyr and SQL, side by side

If you know SQL, this table maps each dplyr verb to the part of the query it
writes. If SQL is new to you, the last column says what each one does.

| dplyr | SQL | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `filter()` | `WHERE` | keeps rows that meet a condition |
| `select()` | `SELECT` | keeps columns |
| `mutate()` | a computed column in `SELECT`, `... AS name` | adds or changes a column |
| `group_by()` + `summarise()` | `GROUP BY`, with `COUNT()`, `AVG()` and so on | one row per group |
| `count()` | `COUNT(*)` with `GROUP BY` | counts rows per group |
| `distinct()` | `SELECT DISTINCT` | drops repeated rows |
| `arrange()` | `ORDER BY` | sorts |
| `inner_join()` | `INNER JOIN` | keeps rows found in both tables |
| `left_join()` | `LEFT JOIN` | adds columns from another table |
| `head(10)` | `LIMIT 10` | keeps the first rows |
| `collect()` | runs the query and fetches every row | brings the result into R |

## Read more

For more on dplyr with databases, read the
[Databases](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/databases.html) chapter of *R for Data
Science*, dbplyr's [introduction](https://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/dbplyr.html)
and its guide to
[function translation](https://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/translation-function.html).

## In short

- Your dplyr code builds one query in R; the database runs it when you print or
  `collect()` it, and only the result comes back. `show_query()` shows its SQL.
- dplyr verbs, and joins between tables on the same connection, run on the
  database. To fetch the records of people you hold in R, use `thip_window()`.
- Inside verbs, use functions dbplyr translates, not your own. THIP's ClickHouse
  treats a few of them differently from the example's DuckDB, so run a new query
  on a small result first.
- `collect()` only small results: filter and summarise first, and count the
  rows when you are not sure.
- `thip_table()` stacks yearly tables and keeps every row. Records add up across
  years but people do not: count people with `n_distinct(pid)` on the stacked
  table.

Next: [From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html) starts the running
question, readmission after appendicitis, and uses `thip_table()` to convert
dates.

DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
